2.t: Not knowing the tune: 'Breeze' at Preservation Hall
2.s: Jim Robinson as melody carrier, and a night when the band struggled with a request.
2.q: out. Yeah I'm not trying to criticize Jim because Jim's my favorite trombonist I'm not trying to make them I don't like his style or anything but there are tunes that he doesn't know there was one tune funny over at Preservation Hall last night Breeze I guess somebody requested the 1920s tune…

615.t: Playing unrehearsed with unfamiliar musicians at parties and in Australia
615.s: He often learns lineups at the last minute; Sydney players fit in after eight bars.
615.q: Not very often I’m glad to say. In fact I can’t think of any time right off. Well when I come to a thing like this, a jazz party, most of the musicians, in fact all of them actually, I’ve known for some years too, so they’re all friends, I just wasn’t sure exactly who was going to be here or what…

535.t: Calling tunes with an unknown rhythm section
535.s: Asked about a pickup rhythm section, he says he might call standards but usually sends his tunes ahead of time.
535.q: Well if I didn’t know the rhythm section at all, yeah maybe I would get a few standards that I would play and you know, but no different than anybody else would do. “It Could Happen to You,” maybe “On Green Dolphin Street” or a ballad or something like that, “I Can’t Get Started” or you know I’d…

985.t: Playing with musicians you've just met: a shared musical language
985.s: Evans explains that a pickup band works because everyone speaks the language of music, with regional dialects like North Philly or the Bronx.
985.q: Well we are a band for tonight. And you know I do hear that a lot, “Oh you’ve just joined them and you guys just met?” Those kinds of things. But I guess that’s what we’ve been doing all our lives practicing and practicing performing music, so then if you’re all speaking that same language, you…

496.t: What to do when a tune is called that you do not know
496.s: Finck says he admits not knowing a song, asks for the chords, and wants to know about reharmonizations.
496.q: After I’ve gotten over my initial panic I always confess I don’t know that song — or I say, “I haven’t played that song in a long time” which is often the case. And I might ask the pianist if he knows it, to just quickly jump through the chords, or if it’s simple enough he’ll go, “all right the…

743.s: Gordon describes playing unrehearsed festival sets, occasionally not knowing bebop melodies, and clarinet taking the first chorus in California.
743.q: Oh on some of them I have. I’ve been at really slick festivals where they are playing some bebop and I’m not too familiar with that type of music and I’ve tried to play it, and I know the chord progressions but maybe the melody I didn’t know. But I’ve been in situations like that yes.

915.t: Playing in unrehearsed jazz party bands and Joe Wilder's tune calling
915.s: Gordon explains the value of a wide repertoire when thrown together with unfamiliar players, and how Joe Wilder called tunes not everyone knew.
915.q: Well that always helps. It always helps to be familiar with a wide range of the jazz repertoire. And you never know, you’re kind of taken out of your comfort zone when you’re at a jazz party and they throw a bunch of different guys together and say okay we’re going to try this. Because you find…

941.t: How musicians build an impromptu concert without sheet music
941.s: Common repertoire and experience let players put together a concert; professionals find common ground, and he prefers to serve the ensemble.
941.q: I guess they don’t — you know there’s a lot of people that forget about the fact that for most of us, it’s common experience that allows us to operate the way we do, you know? And no matter who we work with, and no matter how far removed they are from our usual set of circumstances, the secret is…

520.t: Mouthing while playing and unrehearsed communication with the band
520.s: Hayes did not know he vocalised until seeing video; the Iridium band did not rehearse, relying on the shared language of the music; McPherson arrived late from San Diego.
520.q: No, no. Although sometimes I might be thinking about I’ll be glad when this guy stops soloing. But I think it’s just a facial...

563.t: Calling tunes on the stand and the trumpeter's pressure
563.s: At jazz parties musicians may meet cold; the trumpeter is expected to know and lead the melody.
563.q: Yeah. Sometimes you talk it over beforehand, sometimes you don’t. Sometimes you’re just on the stand and you’d better to know the song they call or else you’re going to be embarrassed or you’re going to be scuffling a little bit. And for the trumpet player it’s a little bit more pressure than the…

808.t: Singing with unfamiliar players at the jazz party
808.s: With Dave Frishberg absent, she must use better-known repertoire with new accompanists, and keeps endings simple so the pianist can fill in.
808.q: Sure. Because Dave and I have a rapport after having worked together for so long, like five and a half years, and I know a lot of obscure songs. That’s kind of what I gravitate to. I don’t do a lot of standards, which sometimes is a disadvantage. So he and I do these obscure songs and we kind of…

415.t: Playing with local rhythm sections; lessons from Sonny Stitt
415.s: Handling unknown bands abroad with common standards, and learning consistency from Sonny Stitt.
415.ch: Opening and the working musician's life
415.q: Sometimes yes, sometimes no. I’ve had to just go right to the job and we have got five minutes. And you really learn how to quickly make decisions. For example there’s common tunes that everybody should know. And if they don’t know those tunes, you’re really in trouble. Like “I Got Rhythm” changes,…

785.t: Stretching 'L-O-V-E' into a nine-minute trio performance
785.s: Rowe asks how Sands turned a short Nat King Cole song into a long performance; Sands talks of expression, journey, listening and taking parts away to change color.
785.q: No. No, I never had to. But if I had to, I mean you know it’s about expression, you know, it’s about a journey, it’s about starting from point A to point B, or point C, D, you know.

163.s: At parties the leader calls tunes; Sherman refreshes unfamiliar ones beforehand.
163.q: Oh well first of all it’s whoever’s the leader on the set, you know, will call the tunes. And oh yeah, once in a while there’ll be something that, very seldom that I never heard of or heard, but I might say oh gee I’m not that familiar with that or that comfortable, or I haven’t played it that…

671.t: Tunes he doesn't know at jam sessions
671.s: If he doesn't know a tune he says so and lets someone else play it.
671.q: You have to really know, you know after I go over it a few times — but on the spur of the moment I don’t do that. If I don’t know it I don’t play it. Let somebody else play it who knows it.

447.t: Not knowing tunes at gigs and the supportive spirit
447.s: Players regularly face unfamiliar tunes, especially bebop heads; musicians help each other.
447.q: Oh sure, sure. This weekend I was a little concerned because there’s a lot of what I would consider more contemporary, modern players here at this, than I’m used to doing on these things. And I’m somewhat a little concerned that the guys are going to start calling up some heavy bebop things and I’m…

425.t: Thinking on your feet with unknown players
425.s: On jazz parties and tours he must size up unfamiliar pianists and keep a large repertoire ready.
425.ch: Life on the road and advice
425.q: You have to be able to think on your feet very quickly. I mean I’ll take a tour in England, I don’t know who I’m going to work with. And I could end up playing somewhere in the middle of the country with a pianist I’ve never seen before, who only knows — I’ve got to be able to look at this guy and…

1049.t: Playing with Roland Hanna at the festival
1049.s: They traded common repertoire such as Autumn Leaves, Footprints and Oye Como Va, and Valentin plans to bring a Latin flavor to the event.
1049.q: No. I think within that timeline there’s something that we know together. And then he just mentioned of course, which I forgot about, like “Autumn Leaves,” and “Carnival” and all those things. So just those two tunes alone could be an hour, depending on the stretch. And then he knew “Footprints,”…

134.t: Visitors who wait all week to play: Billy Foulkes and Henry Pride
134.s: Out-of-town players come to play a prepared tune, sometimes not knowing it.
134.ch: Open sets, touring and Sweet Basil
134.q: They’ll call me up from overseas, and they say, “Get your notebook. I’m coming the second Tuesday in August.” I already got a cat. He’s called me. This cat’s in Australia. He said, “I’ll be there the second Tuesday,” and he gave me his name. I got it written down. He said, “Now I want to play,…
